# Wiki Page Content Rules

Rules bound what a page's body may say: which callouts it may use, how it relates to the code, and, on product pages, which vocabulary it may use.

**See also:** `wiki-conventions` — for how links between pages are formed and resolved.

## Callouts

Callouts give typed in-body emphasis, using Obsidian callout syntax — a blockquote whose first line is `> [!type] Optional title`. They render as colored admonitions in Obsidian and degrade to plain blockquotes elsewhere, so they never cost readability. Optional; `/wiki-conformance-audit` checks the type catalog and the status-field bar.

**Fixed catalog** — use only these; an unrecognized type is out-of-convention:

| Callout | Use for |
|---|---|
| `> [!note]` | A clarifying aside that would otherwise interrupt the prose. |
| `> [!info]` | A scope, context, or provenance note — not the source citation itself, which stays a `[[...]]` link. |
| `> [!warning]` | A pitfall, common misuse, or contradiction the reader must not miss. |
| `> [!quote]` | A verbatim excerpt from a cited source, kept distinct from the page's own voice. |

**Bars:**

- **Status stays in frontmatter.** A callout MUST NOT restate `freshness`, `authorship`, `origination`, or `confidence` — the agent reads those fields directly, and prose copies drift.
- **Callouts never replace a section.** They sit *inside* a page's type-structural H2 sections, never substitute for one.

## Code citations

Citations run one way: code cites the wiki, and a page never points at code. A source file names the page it realizes with `@realizes <domain>:<page-path>`, and a test names the scenario row it proves with `@verifies <subject>#TS<n>`, the subject being the page its `test-scenario` names as the thing under test — each on one comment line in the file's own syntax. A read-only design reference in a repo file names the `ui-surface` or `ui-component` page it illustrates with `@prototypes <domain>:<page-path>`, in whatever comment form its own file has.

**Banned on a page:** a source file's path or name, a link to a source file, and a `file:line` reference. **Exempt are the page types whose subject IS the artifact being cited** — `source-summary`, `synthesis`, `comparison`, `interview-debrief`, `mirror-source` and `study` — because a summary of an external source, or an audit of code, is about that artifact and loses its point without naming it. The exemption follows the type, not the sub-wiki, so it holds wherever one of these pages lives.

**No code symbols:** a page names no class, function, method, or variable that exists only in code. A name in an external contract, such as an API operation, an event, or a table or column other systems use, may appear, except on product pages, where *Code neutrality* still bars it. Describe code by its behavior and role. Leave a product name that ends like a source file (Node.js) unbackticked.

**Why:** a pointer rots silently when its file moves. A citation moves with the file, and a stale one is reported.

## Product sub-wiki authoring

Product pages describe user-facing behavior and commitments in the user's language, not the implementation. Applies to **all `product/` page types** (`feature`, `task-flow`, `product-module`, `persona`, `algorithm`, archive types).

**Code neutrality:** no implementation vocabulary — not column names (`campaignName` → "the campaign's name"), endpoint paths (`/api/v2/campaigns` → "the campaign API"), architectural terms ("the campaign service" → "the campaign list"), or storage-layer qualifiers ("written to PostgreSQL" → "the record is updated").

**Allowed:** a field name that is also the user-facing UI label, in backticks, when the UI literally shows it (e.g. `` `Status` ``). Prefer the plain label where one exists.

**Why:** product pages feed design, integration tests, and agent Q&A. Implementation vocabulary couples them to the codebase — it breaks on rename, misleads designers and researchers, and makes agents cite stale code details as product intent.
